sections.title: Overview
sections.text: One of the tallest antelopes, with the largest horns in the bushbuck tribe (average ~120 cm).

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Eastern and southern Africa.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 120–315 kg; shoulder height 100–150 cm.

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: ~20.8–23 years recorded in captivity.

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: About 9 months (ADW range 7–8.7 months); seasonal breeder in southern Africa, calving when grass is high.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Male calves stay with the maternity herd 1.5–2 years; females longer. Adult males are often solitary or in bachelor groups.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Savanna/woodland and scrub forest with cover.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for specific Texas regions.

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: No verified species-specific stocking rate was found. Carrying capacity depends on rainfall, range condition and competing grazers—get a range/stocking assessment (NRCS or Texas A&M AgriLife).

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: Tropical/subtropical species; no verified cold-tolerance threshold was found. Provide windbreaks and shelter in freezes as a precaution.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Texas Parks & Wildlife states game fences at least 8 ft high (woven-wire or high-tensile) are the only fully reliable deer-exclusion fence. That is the common high-fence standard for deer and antelope; a species-specific minimum for this animal was not found in a primary source.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Browser (leaves, shoots, pods) with some forbs.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: No verified species-specific protein % or mineral formula was found. Texas deer guidance (16–20% CP pellet; 13–16% CP for growth/reproduction) is sometimes used as a reference point but is not antelope-specific—work with a ruminant nutritionist/exotic vet.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Haemonchus contortus and Longistrongylus dominate abomasal worm burdens in free-ranging exotic antelope in Texas (sable, addax, blesbok studied); captive wild ruminants show anthelmintic resistance, so use fecal egg counts and fecal egg-count reduction tests instead of routine blanket deworming.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.text: IUCN Red List: Least Concern.

sections.text: General information, not legal advice. USDA APHIS licensing under the Animal Welfare Act applies to dealers and exhibitors; check USDA and your state wildlife and animal-health agencies before buying, moving or selling.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Tallest land animal; needs specialist husbandry, especially for cold weather.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Sub-Saharan Africa.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: Bulls up to 1,930 kg, cows up to 1,180 kg; 4.7–5.7 m tall; calves 50–55 kg.

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 10–15 years wild; 20–25 years captive (record 27).

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: ~457 days (range 400–468); females breed every 20–30 months; weaning 12–16 months.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Loose herds; females mature at 3–4 years, males breed from ~7 years.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Open savanna/woodland with browse.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: Suitable anywhere in Texas only with a heated barn: AZA/USDA call for heated housing when temperatures average below 50 °F (inference: this occurs statewide in winter). See the interactive Texas species map (../site/map.html).

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: No verified species-specific stocking rate was found. Carrying capacity depends on rainfall, range condition and competing grazers—get a range/stocking assessment (NRCS or Texas A&M AgriLife).

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: AZA: when average daily temperatures fall below 10 °C (50 °F), provide heated housing that holds at least 18 °C (65 °F), with areas near 24 °C (75 °F); measure at chest height of the smallest giraffe. USDA recommends keeping giraffes indoors in cold, inclement weather; a giraffe died in a drafty barn that was ~70°F up high but 45°F lower down. Acclimatized giraffes tolerate heat up to 49 °C (120 °F) with shade.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Follow the AZA Giraffe Care Manual for barrier and barn design; no ranch fence-height figure was verified for this page.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Browser; an adult male can eat up to 66 kg of food per day, surviving on ~7 kg in poor areas.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: Follow the AZA Giraffe Care Manual nutrition chapter; no protein % was verified for this page.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Cold stress/hypothermia is a major documented killer; once chilled, a giraffe struggles to regain body temperature without an outside heat source, and its immune system is compromised. Calves and juveniles are at greatest risk.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: One-humped domesticated camel, highly adapted to heat and water scarcity.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Domesticated; no wild population. Kept across North Africa, the Middle East and beyond.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 300–690 kg; males ~10% heavier than females (males 400–600 kg).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 40–50 years in captivity (max ~50).

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Hot, dry climates. Tolerates >30% water loss and can drink ~100 L in 10 minutes; body temperature varies daily from ~34 °C to 41 °C to save water.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: INFERRED only: desert-adapted (see Habitat needs), so the arid Trans-Pecos/Chihuahuan Desert is the closest climate match; no Texas county distribution data found. See the interactive Texas species map (../site/map.html).

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: Scottish DWA guidance (minimum, zoo/licence context): one camel ≥5×10 m; one male + two females ≥10×20 m. Pasture-kept animals need far more.

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: Provide a shelter large enough for all animals, sited against the worst prevailing weather, plus shade through all daylight hours; lockable shelter recommended.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Wire mesh, visible high-tensile wire or post-and-rail at least 1.9 m (6 ft); mesh must not entangle heads or legs; barbed wire is not appropriate.

AgriLife cites ~6–7% CP for rumen maintenance and 13–16% CP for growth, antler production and reproduction (white-tailed deer data; applied to exotic deer by analogy). Mineral program: set with a nutritionist/vet; no verified species figure.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Haemonchus contortus and Longistrongylus dominate abomasal worm burdens in free-ranging exotic antelope in Texas (sable, addax, blesbok studied); captive wild ruminants show anthelmintic resistance, so use fecal egg counts and fecal egg-count reduction tests instead of routine blanket deworming.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.title: Conservation status
sections.text: IUCN Red List: Least Concern.

sections.title: Legal notes (general info, not legal advice)
sections.text: In Texas, exotic CWD-susceptible species (elk, red deer, sika and others) must carry official ID, have movements reported to TAHC within 48 hours, and eligible mortalities tested; TAHC ended its voluntary CWD Herd Certification Program on Sept 16, 2025. General information, not legal advice. USDA APHIS licensing under the Animal Welfare Act applies to dealers and exhibitors; check USDA and your state wildlife and animal-health agencies before buying, moving or selling.
